intro.heading: You audit what the library asks. You need what your people need.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager runs a small service supporting adults with learning disabilities and autism. Her team already runs audits every month, and the scores look healthy. But when she reads the questions, none of them ask whether each person's communication passport is followed, whether the sensory space is set up the way each person likes, or whether a planned routine change was explained in the way that person understands. Those are the things that make a good day or a bad day in her service. The audit checklist everyone uses is sound, and it is not hers. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The team completes its audits on time and the scores are good.
Each person has a detailed support plan and a communication passport.
Staff care about how each person likes their day to go.
The manager reads the audit questions and none ask about passports or routines.
A new carer has never been checked against one person's sensory preferences.
A spreadsheet of her own questions sits outside the audit system.
Scores in one place, the questions that matter in another.
“How do you know staff follow each person's plan?” The audits do not say.

trail_close: The audits were never wrong. They were written for services in general, and yours is particular. Here is how CareStream lets you keep the library and add questions of your own.

why.heading: A generic checklist cannot know what your service stands for
why.sub: The most useful audit is the one that checks the things you promised the people you support.

cards.title: Specialist care has specialist questions
cards.body: Communication passports, sensory needs, planned routines and positive behaviour support are different in every service. A broad checklist can only ask about them in general terms.

cards.title: Good scores can hide a blind spot
cards.body: If the questions never touch your highest risk areas, a high score tells you very little about them. It only shows that the questions asked were answered well.

cards.title: A side spreadsheet is a risk of its own
cards.body: Questions kept outside the audit system have no scores, no photos, no actions and no history. Nobody can see whether the same problem keeps coming back.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them

items.q: Why would I build a custom audit when there are over 100 in the library?
items.a: You might not need to. The library covers a lot of ground, and a small edit can fix many gaps. But if your service has routines, risks or promises that no library audit asks about, building your own lets you ask exactly those questions and still get scores, photos, actions and a PDF report.

items.q: Can every plan build its own audit?
items.a: No. Building your own audit is on the Enterprise plan. Every other plan can preview any audit and make small edits to a built in one: reword questions, change question types and add up to 2 questions. Anything bigger needs the Enterprise builder.

items.q: What do I get on the Free plan?
items.a: The whole library of more than 100 audits, with scoring, photos, a PDF report, actions, scheduling and optional manager approval. Recommendations from our own machine learning are paid plans only. The library is a good place to start while you decide.

items.q: I already have an audit in Word. Do I have to retype it?
items.a: On Enterprise you can import it from a PDF, Word file, text file or photo, up to 15 MB. CareStream drafts the questions and you review and edit before saving. Importing uses tokens from your monthly allowance. Check every question, because a draft is only a draft.

Anyone you allocate it to. In Staff, set the access level to Staff + Audits and tick the audits that person can conduct. It is per person, not by group or role. They run it in the Staff Hub on a phone, tablet or desktop. Scheduling an audit to someone also allocates it to them.

You can add an action with an owner, a priority and a due date, and the owner can add up to 10 photos as proof when it is done. At the next audit of the same kind, the earlier actions come up for the auditor to mark fixed or not fixed. A reopened action goes back to its owner by email.

items.q: Does the score tell me our CQC rating?
items.a: No. The score is CareStream's own measure of your answers. It is not a CQC rating, and an audit is not a record that goes to the regulator. It helps you spot weak areas and show that you check. See your CQC evidence for how it fits together.

Create a free account and run a library audit today. Building your own is on Enterprise, so if you want to test it with your own questions, book a demo or start the 14 day free trial on a paid plan and talk to us about Enterprise. See the pricing page for plan details.

limits.heading: A tool for your questions, not a replacement for your judgement

cards.title: Building your own is Enterprise only
cards.body: Other plans can make small edits to a built in audit: reword, change types and add up to 2 questions. A full build needs Enterprise.

cards.title: It does not decide what is good practice
cards.body: CareStream drafts and scores what you write. Whether the questions match your policy, your regulator's expectations and your people's needs is your call.

cards.title: Scores are ours, not a rating
cards.body: An audit score is not a CQC rating and the audit is not a regulator submitted record. Recommendations are on the paid plans, not the Free plan.

items.a: This is a set of questions you write yourself, instead of using a ready made template. In CareStream it runs like any other audit, with scoring by section, photo evidence, actions and a PDF report.

An audit checklist is a list of questions an auditor answers while looking at a service, such as yes, no or N/A. A good audit checklist is specific, easy to answer and tied to something you can fix. A digital one adds scores, photos and a history.

items.q: Are digital audits better than paper?
items.a: They are easier to score, repeat and compare. A guide to digital audits covers the detail. The real gain is that findings turn into actions that someone owns, and the next audit checks them.

items.q: Is there an audit tool that is free?
items.a: Audits are free to run on every plan, including the Free plan, with more than 100 to choose from. They have scoring, photos, a PDF report, actions and scheduling. Writing your own questions from scratch is the Enterprise feature.

items.q: Can I edit a built in audit on a lower plan?
items.a: Yes, in a small way. You can reword questions, change question types and add up to 2 questions. The first edit makes the audit your own copy and hides the built in one.

items.q: Which library audits suit a learning disability service?
items.a: The library has audits labelled for learning disability and autism services, covering areas such as positive behaviour support, consent and health access. Start with medicines management or the safeguarding log review, and browse the rest at the audit library.

items.q: Does a care audit satisfy CQC?
items.a: There is no single audit that does. Regulation 17 says systems must be established and operated effectively so you can assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the services provided. A care audit is one way to show you do that, alongside action on what it finds.

items.q: What does the law say about assessing risk?
items.a: Regulation 12 says care and treatment must be provided safely, which includes assessing the risks to the health and safety of service users and doing all that is reasonably practicable to mitigate them. Your own questions can check that your risk controls are being followed.

guide.heading: How to write a good custom audit
guide.lede: Your own audit is only as useful as its questions. Whether you build it from scratch or edit a library audit, a few habits keep it practical.

sections.h3: Start from what could go wrong for the people you support
paragraphs: List the five or six things that matter most in your service, such as communication, routines, sensory needs, medicines changes and consent. Then ask what an auditor could see, check or count that would show each one is working. Those observable things become your questions.
Compare your list with the library first. If a built in audit already asks, copy it and adjust it. Keep your own questions for the gaps, so your audit tool stays short enough to finish.

sections.h3: Check each question before it goes live
checklist: Can an auditor answer it by looking, asking or checking a record, without guessing?
Does it have one clear answer type, such as yes or no, a number or a rating?
Is it tied to something you can fix, and does a failed answer have an owner?
Is it ever not relevant? If so, allow N/A or a condition so it does not unfairly lower the score.

sections.h3: Run it, then review the audit itself
paragraphs: After the first run, read the answers. Questions everyone passes may be too easy. Questions that confuse auditors need rewording. Each edit creates a new version, so the history shows when and why you changed what you ask.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the scores, the photos and the closed actions together, so you can show that you check the things that matter to your service and that you act on what you find.
